author: Marty Neumeier
concept: A brand is a person's gut feeling, not what you say it is
summary: Neumeier defines a brand not as a logo, an identity system, or a product, but as a person's gut feeling about a product, service, or company. Because it lives in other people's minds, a brand is not what you say it is, it is what they say it is; when enough individuals converge on the same gut feeling, a brand exists.
usable_principle: Treat the brand as market perception you influence but do not own; manage the gut feeling in the audience's mind rather than the message you broadcast.
sniped_relevance: For BJ this reframes any brand question as: what gut feeling forms in the market, not what claim is made; the work and the proof shape perception more than the assertion. author: Marty Neumeier
concept: The brand gap and the charismatic brand: bridging strategy and creativity
summary: Neumeier names the brand gap as the chasm between left-brain strategy (logic) and right-brain creativity (magic); brands fail at the point of contact when the two are not bridged. Brands that close the gap become charismatic (a product for which people believe there is no substitute), and aesthetics is the bridge because it is the language of feeling in an information-rich, time-poor world.
usable_principle: Bridge logic and magic deliberately; use aesthetics as a strategic asset (the language of feeling) that resists commoditization, not as decoration.
sniped_relevance: BJ's visual craft is strategic leverage here: aesthetics done with intent shrinks the psychic distance to an audience and resists being commoditized, held as a tool not a lifestyle. author: Marty Neumeier
concept: The five disciplines and the three differentiation questions
summary: Neumeier organizes brand-building into five disciplines: differentiate, collaborate, innovate, validate, and cultivate. Differentiation starts with three blunt questions every brand must answer cleanly: who are you, what do you do, and why does it matter, with the third being the hardest and most decisive.
usable_principle: Earn a brand by answering who-you-are, what-you-do, and why-it-matters cleanly, then differentiate, collaborate, innovate, validate, and cultivate as a repeatable discipline.

author: David Airey
concept: The brief as the structural framework that disciplines the work
summary: Across the studios Airey interviews, the creative brief is the structural framework that keeps a project honest: agreed up front, it becomes the benchmark every creative route is judged against, so subjective preference (a CEO who dislikes blue) is overruled by whether the work serves the agreed objectives. concept: The naming process: brief, generate many, narrow, screen, commit
summary: Meyerson lays out the professional naming process as a repeatable, iterative discipline: write a naming brief, generate hundreds of candidates, whittle to a finalist set, prescreen for trademark and run linguistic checks, then build consensus and make the commitment.
